items.prompt: White to move. Count the white pieces that defend the square g4 in this position.

claims.statement: No white piece defends g4.
Two black pieces attack g4.

hints: Which white pieces could reach g4 in one move?
The queen's diagonal d1-g4 passes through f3.
None: the knight on f3 blocks the queen.
items.explain: The queen on d1 would see g4 along the diagonal d1-e2-f3-g4, but its own knight stands on f3. The knight attacks other squares. So g4 is defended by nothing, and a pawn there would be captured for free.

items.prompt: Black is in check from the knight. Find a safe king move.

claims.statement: At depth 16 g8 and e8 are within 40 centipawns.
The move to e6 loses at least 450 centipawns.

hints: The king has three squares: g8, e8 and e6.
Which one walks onto the open diagonal in front of the bishop?
The corner g8 or the back rank e8 are both fine.
items.explain: The king on g8 or e8 stays near its pieces, off the diagonal from c4. On e6 the king is in the open: Bc4+ comes with tempo and the queen follows. This lesson follows 8...Kg8, because both moves are rated almost equal and g8 is the more common choice in our data.

feedback_by_move.f7e6: The king walks into the centre: the bishop check comes with tempo and the engine sees a swing of more than five pawns.

items.prompt: Black has walked the king to e6. White to move. Find White's strongest move.

claims.statement: At depth 16 the bishop check is the best move.
White is clearly ahead (depth 16).

hints: The king is in the open on e6.
Which white piece can check along a diagonal?
The bishop goes to c4.
items.explain: The bishop reaches c4 with check along the diagonal to e6; the only block is the knight, and then the queen lines up on the e-file behind the knight on e5.

items.prompt: Black is in check from the bishop. Find the best reply.

claims.statement: At depth 16 ...Nd5 is the best reply.
The pawn block gives up at least 50 centipawns.
The king step to h7 gives up at least 150 centipawns.
The queen block loses at least 700 centipawns.
The bishop block ...Be6 loses at least 700 centipawns.

hints: Five replies are legal: compare what each leaves behind.
Which block leaves your e-pawn and your f5 bishop free to move?
The knight goes to d5.
items.explain: The knight on d5 blocks the diagonal, is defended by the c6 pawn and the queen, and leaves the e-pawn free. The pawn block ...e6 is playable but allows g4 with a real attack (see the next boards). The king step to h7 gives the edge back, and the queen block loses the queen.

feedback_by_move.e7e6: Playable, but g4 is the answer: the bishop on f5 is attacked and the edge shrinks to a few tenths of a pawn.
feedback_by_move.g8h7: The king gives up the corner and the engine sees the edge disappear.
feedback_by_move.d8d5: Bxd5 cxd5 (or Nxd5) wins the queen for a bishop.
feedback_by_move.f5e6: Bxe6+ Kh7 and White mates in four; the bishop is the only guard of the king's diagonal.

items.prompt: White to move. No move wins by force here; pick any sensible developing move.

claims.statement: At depth 16 Qe4, Ng6, O-O, Bd2 and Qe2 are within 40 centipawns of each other.
Black is ahead by more than one pawn whatever White chooses (depth 16).

hints: There is no single refutation here.
Look for development or activity: the queen, the knight, the king.
Qe4, Qe2, Ng6, O-O and Bd2 are all rated within 40 centipawns.
items.explain: None of these moves wins material; they are different ways to keep developing, and the key lists every sensible move the engine rates about equally (Qe4, Qe2, Ng6, O-O, Bd2). At depth 16 Black remains about one and a half pawns ahead, which is why Black's side of this line is easy to play.

items.prompt: White to move after 9...e6. Is the pawn move to g4 White's best move?

claims.statement: At depth 16 g4 is the best move.
Two white pieces defend g4 after the pawn move.
Two black pieces attack g4.

hints: Count the defenders of g4 after the pawn lands there.
The knight left f3, so the queen's diagonal is open.
Yes: two defenders against two attackers, and the pawn hits the bishop.
items.explain: The pawn is attacked by the bishop and the knight and defended by the queen and the knight. Because the pawn itself attacks the bishop, Black has no time for a capture sequence that loses material. The engine rates g4 clearly best.

items.prompt: Black to move after g4. The bishop is attacked. Find a good reply.

claims.statement: At depth 16 ...b5 and ...Be4 are within 40 centipawns.
After ...Bh7 White mates in one with the bishop capture on e6.
The bishop move to g6 loses at least 400 centipawns.
The knight capture on g4 gives up at least 50 centipawns.

hints: Which squares keep the bishop safe, and what happens to e6?
Only a few replies do not lose at once.
Either hit the bishop on c4 first with ...b5, or move the bishop to e4.
items.explain: Two replies hold: ...b5 attacks the bishop on c4 first, and ...Be4 gives up the pawn on e6 for activity. The bishop move to h7 is mate in one, and the move to g6 loses the bishop to the knight.

feedback_by_move.f5g6: The knight takes the bishop and the engine sees more than five pawns for White.
feedback_by_move.f6g4: Nxg4 and the engine sees the edge turn into a small White advantage.

items.prompt: White to move after ...Bg4. Does Ne5+ win the bishop?

claims.statement: Two white pieces attack g4 after the knight move.
One black piece defends g4.
At depth 16 Ne5+ is the best move.

hints: Which squares does a knight on e5 attack?
It attacks g4. The queen on d1 also sees g4 once the f3 knight moves.
Yes: two attackers against one defender.
items.explain: The knight on e5 attacks g4 and gives check at the same time, and the queen joins along the open diagonal. Two attackers against one defender wins the bishop.

items.prompt: White to move after ...Bf5. Name the squares a knight on e5 attacks. Does Ne5+ win the bishop?

claims.statement: A knight on e5 attacks these squares (f5 is not among them).

hints: Which squares does a knight on e5 attack?
Count the knight's eight jumps from e5.
No: f5 is not one of them.
items.explain: A knight on e5 attacks c4, c6, d3, d7, f3, f7, g4 and g6. The bishop on f5 is not on the list, so the check wins nothing by itself.

items.prompt: White to move after ...Bd7. Count the attackers and defenders of d7. Is Ne5+ winning material?

claims.statement: After the knight move one white piece attacks d7.
Three black pieces defend d7: queen, knight and knight.

hints: Count attackers and defenders of d7.
One attacker against several defenders wins nothing.
No: three defenders against one attacker.
items.explain: The knight attacks d7 once, while the queen and both knights defend it. Capturing would only trade a knight for a bishop. A check that attacks a piece is a fork only if the target is undefended or outnumbered.

items.prompt: White to move after 8...Kg8. Find the move the engine rates first.

claims.statement: At depth 16 Bc4+ is the best move.

hints: There is a check that develops a piece.
The bishop checks along the open diagonal.
The bishop goes to c4.
items.explain: The bishop reaches c4 with check and develops at the same time; the quiet developing moves are rated much lower at depth 16.
